title: How to read a study
hookLine: ask who was studied, how many, and compared to what

cards: Here's a headline, made up but familiar. Study finds people who meditate are twenty percent happier. It sounds settled.
It has a number. It says study. But hiding behind that one sentence are three questions that decide whether it means anything at all.
You don't need a lab coat or a statistics class to ask them. You need about ten seconds and a little stubbornness.

teach.b: Question one: who was studied? A huge share of psychology research has been done on university students in wealthy Western countries.

In 2010 three researchers, Joseph Henrich, Steven Heine and Ara Norenzayan, pointed out that these people are unusual on many measures compared with humanity as a whole, and gave them a memorable nickname, WEIRD: Western, educated, industrialized, rich and democratic.
A result from twenty-year-old psychology majors might hold for a grandmother in Lagos. Or it might not. Question two: how many?
Small studies bounce around. Flip a coin ten times and seven heads isn't strange. Flip it a thousand times and seven hundred heads would be.
A study with twenty people can find a big effect by luck; the same effect in two thousand people is much less likely to be luck.
Question three, the one that matters most: compared to what? If people who meditate are happier, maybe meditation helped. Or maybe happier, calmer people are the ones who take up meditation.

Or maybe they have more free time, or more money. That's why the strongest studies randomly assign people, one group practices and one doesn't, so the groups start out alike. Even then, ask what the other group did.
Nothing, or something else that also takes time and attention, like exercise or a class?

teach.h: BEATING NOTHING IS A LOW BAR.
teach.b: Beating nothing is a low bar.
Beating a real alternative is the real test. None of this makes you a cynic. It makes you fair.

how: Careful readers of health research look at the sample, its size, and whether there was a randomized comparison group, especially an active one, before trusting a headline.

o: a nickname for the narrow samples psychology often studies
a warning sign for studies paid for by big companies
a label for odd results that no other lab can repeat

games.q: reading a study — tap the pairs.

s: a study with a number in the headline is settled
ask who, how many, and compared to what first.
small studies can find big effects by luck
like seven heads in ten coin flips.
beating a group that did nothing is the strongest test
beating a real alternative, like exercise or a class, is the stronger test.

games.q: people who meditate turn out to be happier. what's one other explanation?
o: happier, calmer people may be the ones who take up meditation.
games.why: without random assignment, the arrow might point the other way; that's why the best studies randomize.

practice: Turn the three questions on the practice you held in mind yesterday: who's in your study (just you, one person), how many days you've tried it (a handful, or a season), and compared to what (days without it, or just your hopes).
No judgment; only notice what you'd need to know. Then let the questions rest, and breathe.
